rationale: VIVI-OLIVE registers falls and gait for a diet-plus-extra-virgin-oil bundle. The Buriram study gives a timed mobility comparison for cannabis in a common olive carrier. The six-person series documents baseline postural instability only. An isolated cold-pressed oil effect on clinical Parkinson postural instability remains unresolved.

The extra-virgin versus refined trial outside Parkinson disease gives a favorable 4.22-point adjusted constipation difference. The mixed-diet Parkinson trials have inconclusive bowel contrasts. The Lithuanian adjusted association is for a composite dietary score, with no separated oil grade. The weak favorable lean continues to rely on the grade-specific non-Parkinson comparison.

The small baseline Parkinson and independent non-Parkinson observational estimates weakly favor lower anxiety, with confounding and multiplicity limits. The Lithuanian adjusted result is for a composite diet. The distinct KIM and diabetes programs do not isolate olive oil. The Buriram article and registration represent one trial with olive oil shared by both arms, leaving a minimal favorable lean grounded in the earlier observations.

Baseline Parkinson walking difficulty is inversely associated with unspecified olive oil. Timed-walk comparisons in obesity and sarcopenia remain inconclusive. The single Buriram cohort gives no clear difference in gait velocity after cannabinoids were added to the shared sublingual oil vehicle. PRIME has planned mobility outcomes. Cold-pressed olive oil and clinical Parkinson walking speed remain unresolved.

A baseline graphic gives a weak inverse estimate for pooled tremor with ungraded olive oil. A whole ketogenic diet reports early worsening in a combined tremor-or-rigidity measure. A cannabinoid randomized trial reports only a composite motor result, and a six-person series gives baseline tremor only. Neither resolves a rest-tremor effect for extra-virgin olive oil.

The small baseline association with movement slowness gives a minimal favorable lean as a bradykinesia proxy. Whole-diet motor evidence is mixed. The randomized Buriram study measured a composite, and the smaller cannabis case series records bradykinesia at baseline. Both use common ungraded carriers without an oil-specific contrast.

The walnut-oil milkshake trial measures laboratory fear extinction and has a secondary report of an inconclusive overall mood comparison. Its clinical depression subscale and grade remain unverified. The diabetes protocol offers optional walnut oil and plans a depression scale but reports no verified oil-specific outcome. Cold-pressed walnut oil and Parkinson depressive symptoms remain unresolved.

Oral comparator arms using peanut oil show some within-arm improvement in depression scores. These include healthy volunteers, irritable bowel syndrome and a vitamin D trial, all without an independent refined-oil comparison. The peanut-only arm of a topical and inhalational trial also improved. Planned diabetes program depression results are unavailable. These exposures and populations leave direction unresolved for refined peanut oil in Parkinson disease.

The oral comparator gives no clear within-arm anxiety change and differs from roasted peanuts. Topical peanut carrier reports and a composite mouse oil substitution give no independent human oil contrast. The diabetes support trial reports only program-level anxiety. Cold-pressed peanut oil and clinical Parkinson anxiety remain unresolved.

Sleep comparator and population studies give indirect evidence. Both KIM diet phases encouraged unspecified olive oil, and an insomnia event concerned the overall diet. A six-person cannabis series gives a within-dose insomnia improvement with shared ungraded olive oil. Neither gives an independent extra-virgin oil effect on Parkinson insomnia.
